Done

Okay, pulled the picture together — here's where things stand and the two things you asked for.

Status check (from your most recent chat, today): PANEL_SPEC.md is at v1.3, five sections locked (Goal, Direction, Decisions, Timeline, HOW), Stage 4 computation spec is written and has run on real Style-DNA data (Direction 21.7%/78.3%, HOW=COPILOT), and you just finished a deep-dive comparing your pipeline against the official CoTrace repo. The Timeline section specifically: collapsed delta bar + drawer that opens into a cropped SVG trace-exchange block, per-turn chip colors, two-level expansion with a "proof layer." That's the part your P1/P2/P3 question is about.

1. What your panel solves in co-creative systems generally

The COTRACE paper's own user study handed you the exact failure modes a general-purpose agency panel needs to fix, straight from their participants:

P8: "The tool said I did nothing... it doesn't see the cognitive work of choosing between the items." — Automatic post-hoc scoring is blind to evaluation work (comparing, selecting, rejecting options) because that work leaves no artifact trace. Your open-slot + user-marking mechanism is the direct fix: the act of marking a turning point asserts cognitive work an automatic scorer can't see. That's not a COTRACE-specific fix, it's a fix for any system that scores contribution from outputs alone.

P7: confused about how a 50% vs 55% split was calculated at a granular level, wanted a disclaimer/info panel. — Your drawer's "proof layer" (showing the actual trace exchange behind a delta) is the general answer: contribution measurement is illegible unless the user can drill into the evidence, not just the number.

P6: didn't find the flagged "indirect influence" meaningful — the tool's judgment of what counts as a contribution didn't match the user's own sense of significance. — This is the strongest case for your live, in-conversation, user-adjustable design over a post-hoc verdict: significance is subjective and shifts turn to turn, so it can't be fixed once by an algorithm after the fact.

The paradoxes paper's Ambiguity vs. Precision and Control vs. Serendipity tensions map onto the same thing: any system trying to make AI contribution legible has to do it without forcing premature precision on ambiguous, still-forming ideas, and without taking away the user's ability to let the AI surprise them. A live reflective mirror that never blocks action (vs. a verdict that closes the loop) is the general design pattern that resolves both.

So the transferable claim for your panel, beyond your own thesis, is: contribution-visibility tools fail when they're (a) output-only, (b) opaque about their math, and (c) post-hoc/final. Your architecture attacks all three at once — marking-in-the-moment fixes (a), the drawer fixes (b), live-and-ongoing fixes (c). That's a generalizable claim you could state independent of Idea 4's specific UI.

2. Analogies for the "turn markers on a timeline" mechanism

A few different families, each teaching something different:

ESPN/sports win-probability graphs (per-play swing between two teams) — closest structural analogy to your delta bar. It's literally two parties, a running score, and a line that swings per discrete event. The lesson to borrow: those charts work because the swing itself is the story ("this one play changed everything"), not the cumulative total — worth checking your delta bar leads with per-turn swing, not just cumulative %.

Chess engine eval bars + move-by-move analysis (chess.com, Lichess) — a vertical bar shifting per move, with click-to-expand showing the position/reasoning. Very close to your two-level expansion (bar → drawer with proof). Difference: theirs judges "who's winning," yours judges "who acted" — worth being explicit that you're not doing a quality judgment, just an agency one, since users pattern-match eval bars to "good/bad."

Git commit graphs / GitLens blame — per-commit authorship, expandable diffs, blame-by-line. This is the closest existing "who did what, when, expandable to proof" pattern in a tool developers already trust, and a good citation if a reviewer asks "hasn't this been done."

DAW automation lanes (Ableton, Logic) — keyframed values over a timeline, collapsed lane vs. expanded curve. Useful mainly for the interaction pattern of collapse/expand you're already using.

Track Changes / Google Docs version history with named checkpoints — closest "human edits vs. accepted-as-is" precedent, but it's artifact-only (no conversation trace), which is exactly the DraftMarks/Cursor Agent Trace gap your handoff doc already flagged.

YouTube/podcast chapter markers and Loom timeline comments — good precedent for user-placed markers on a timeline (your bookmark/turning-point mechanic), though those are just navigation aids, not attribution.

Your existing academic precedents (HaLLMark, CoAuthorViz, DocuViz, OnGoal) already cover the closest scholarly matches — CoAuthorViz and DocuViz both do turn-by-turn authorship coloring on a timeline, OnGoal does goal-tracking over a conversation. Those remain your strongest direct citations; the sports/chess/git analogies above are better for justifying design choices (why a bar, why two-level expansion, why per-turn swing) than for the literature review itself.

The one thing none of these combine that yours does: a live agency split (not authorship, not version history, not eval) with a click-through proof layer, updating turn-by-turn inside the chat itself. That combination is still the gap, which is good news for the "how is this novel" section of your writeup.
